summary:
First Outpost is an interactive 3D educational simulation developed in response to NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: “Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer.”

Our browser-based game allows players to manage their own lunar or Martian outpost through realistic space missions. Players must make critical decisions about energy distribution, life support, food production, scientific research and radiation protection, experiencing the consequences of their choices.

What makes First Outpost unique is its integration of real NASA data rather than fictional scenarios. We use NASA DONKI space-weather records, Curiosity's REMS and RAD measurements, and NASA JPL planetary positions to recreate historical space conditions and their impact on missions.

The platform also features an interactive 3D environment, resource collection, construction, scientific experiments, multiplayer missions for up to four players, and an educational assistant named Lumi.

First Outpost makes complex space science accessible through hands-on learning, helping children develop scientific curiosity, critical thinking and decision-making skills while understanding the real challenges of future human exploration beyond Earth.
details:
Project Details — First Outpost

First Outpost is an interactive 3D educational simulation developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 under the challenge "Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer." It allows players to experience the challenges of managing a human outpost on Mars or at the Moon's south pole during missions lasting 6 or 10 weeks.

How It Works

Each in-game week represents a new stage of the mission. Players receive a limited amount of energy and must distribute it between four essential systems: life support, the greenhouse, the laboratory and radiation protection. They also face unexpected events based on real space exploration challenges. Every decision has consequences, which are explained through weekly reports and a final mission review.

The simulation incorporates real NASA data rather than relying entirely on fictional scenarios. We use NASA's DONKI database for solar flares and radiation storms, Curiosity's REMS instrument for Martian temperature measurements, Curiosity's RAD instrument for radiation data, and NASA JPL planetary positions to calculate Earth–Mars distances and communication delays. These datasets directly influence mission conditions and gameplay events.

Players can also explore an interactive 3D environment, conduct spacewalks, collect regolith and metal, drive a rover, construct new buildings and complete scientific experiments. The platform includes a multiplayer mode supporting up to four players, allowing friends to manage the same mission together.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Our main goal is to make space science more accessible and engaging. Instead of simply reading about space exploration, players learn by making decisions and experiencing their consequences. The game introduces concepts such as radiation exposure, resource management, planetary environments, space communication and food production beyond Earth.

We aim to encourage scientific curiosity, critical thinking, teamwork and responsible decision-making while helping players better understand the scientific and engineering challenges of future human exploration.

Technologies and Tools

The project was developed using TypeScript, Preact and Vite, with Three.js powering the interactive 3D environment. Our mission simulation logic is separated from the graphical interface, allowing its rules to be independently tested and balanced. Supabase Realtime enables multiplayer functionality.

We also use Blender scripts to procedurally generate our 3D models, while ElevenLabs text-to-speech was used to create pre-recorded English and Russian voice narration. The application is deployed on Vercel and can be accessed directly through a web browser without installation or registration.

Creativity and Design Considerations

What makes First Outpost creative is the combination of real scientific datasets, resource-management mechanics and an interactive 3D space environment in one educational experience. Historical solar storms, actual Martian temperatures and changing communication delays become meaningful gameplay challenges rather than just scientific facts displayed on a screen.

We also designed the experience to make complex scientific concepts easier to understand. The game includes short explanations, interactive science facts, recorded narration, three text sizes, colour-blind accessibility patterns and an educational robot assistant called Lumi. Lumi uses predefined, reviewed explanations rather than generating answers through an AI chatbot.

During development, our team considered scientific accuracy, age-appropriate complexity, accessibility, device performance, replayability and player privacy. We wanted to create an experience that is scientifically meaningful without becoming too complicated or overwhelming.
